blocks.text: The immune system is not in one place: it is made of many individual cells that rush to the site of infection. These are white blood cells, which arise in the bone marrow and circulate in blood and lymph, and are also found in the lymph nodes, spleen, liver, thymus and bone marrow. There are three main kinds: monocytes, T cells and B cells; T and B cells together are called lymphocytes.

blocks.text: Monocytes are produced in the bone marrow. They circulate in the blood and enter the interstitial fluid, where they mature into macrophages that engulf and destroy microbes and make proteins that activate helper T cells. Monocytes also mature into other phagocytes that stay in the liver, spleen, lymph nodes and other tissues, and help clear cell debris and repair tissue damage.

T cells develop from stem cells in the bone marrow and migrate to the thymus, a small grey gland just above the heart, where they mature and learn to identify foreign molecules (antigens) on invading microbes. Tens of millions of different T cells are made, each specialised to recognise one particular antigen, so no invader escapes being recognised by at least a few.

blocks.text: B cells also develop in the bone marrow but do not go to the thymus; they complete their maturation in the bone marrow and are then released into the blood and lymph. Each B cell, like a T cell, recognises a particular antigen. When it meets its antigen it divides into many plasma cells, each producing an antibody that sticks to the antigen and marks it for destruction.
